blocks.text: 2.5 Spatial and infrastructure readiness
Tourism readiness falls with every step away from Cape Town, so growth outside the Metro depends on deliberate corridor investment rather than spillover.
The tourism economy and who shares in it

The supply-side evidence in this section and the next starts from the same fact: the tourism economy is large and concentrated. Foreign visitors spent R25.9bn in the province in FY2025 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p11), and the Cape Metro generates 72.5% of provincial GDPR (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p39).

Little of that spend reaches the communities around the nodes. The 20 communities shortlisted by the inclusion work hold 18.4% of the province's residents (Census 2011) but receive a traced floor of 0.02% to 0.04% of foreign direct spend, about R4m to R10m a year (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p5). Section 2.5 sets out where the supply sits; section 2.6 sets out why so little of it is shared.
What was asked

The supply phase was asked to understand spatial infrastructure and readiness for scalable growth through an asset inventory and readiness index, GIS mapping, regional profiles and an investment opportunity framework (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p11, p18). This work answers SLA Annexure B clauses 1.1.2, 1.1.8 and 3.2.4. [Clause wording to be checked against the signed Annexure B.]
What was done

The Infrastructure Report mapped 50,332 tourism assets across the six regions in three layers: attractions, services and enabling infrastructure (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p2, p9, p10). It drew on Wesgro's supply database, SANParks and CapeNature data and open geographic sources (p4). Its premise is that "destination performance is constrained by the weakest layer" (p9).

Each region is scored from 1 to 5 on attractiveness (40%), readiness and capacity (30%) and accessibility (30%) (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p17). The scores "are evidence informed, not purely formula derived", and missing data is not scored as poor performance (p18). The overall ratings are the Infrastructure Report's evidence-informed judgement, not a weighted formula, so this report does not re-derive them.

Six touring routes were rated Ready, Developing or Gap on access, accommodation, safety and bookability (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p19). The final report of July 2026 supersedes a June draft. [Dataset limits, including the absence of geography below district level, to be confirmed against the supply dataset notes.]
Findings that survived into the tree

**1. Readiness halves between the Metro and the periphery.** The Cape Metro rates 4.5 out of 5, the Cape Winelands and the Garden Route 3.4, the Overberg 2.7, the West Coast 2.5 and the Central Karoo 1.9 (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p28, p41, p52, p63, p74, p85). The report's summary is blunt: infrastructure is "eroding rapidly with distance from Cape Town, weakening the visitor experience" (p5).

Accessibility falls fastest (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p88 to p90). On attractions it scores 4.7 in the Metro, 3.3 in the Winelands and 3.0 on the Garden Route. It drops to 2.0 in the Overberg, 1.7 on the West Coast and 1.0 in the Central Karoo; on transport the Metro scores 5.0. "The further from Cape Town, the faster the infrastructure falls away" (p90).

blocks.text: **2. Cape Town is the gateway and the dispersal point.** The Metro holds 20,281 of the 50,332 assets, 40.3%, and five of the province's six highest-volume attractions (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p23, p88). It is the only region with an international airport and rapid transit (p90). The report concludes that "dispersal needs deliberate corridor investment, not organic spillover from Cape Town" (p5).

blocks.caption: Each district has a distinct strength, and the Metro holds two in every five of the province's tourism assets.
blocks.source: Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026: asset counts p23, p34, p45, p56, p67, p78 (Winelands share computed: 7,730 of 50,332 is 15.4%); strengths and weaknesses p88 to p90.

blocks.text: **3. Beyond the Metro and the Garden Route the visitor drives.** Public transport is "effectively absent" on the West Coast and in the Overberg, the Winelands have no transit between estates or valleys, and every accessibility measure in the Central Karoo "sits at the floor" (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p49, p90). Metro rail is "functionally unusable for tourism" (p90).

**4. Strong assets sit in cold zones.** The West Coast has the province's highest natural-asset attractiveness and the Central Karoo its most unique niche assets, yet both score lowest on readiness (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p88). Inland areas north of the N2 on the Garden Route are tourism-inactive, and industrial belts in the Metro show "zero tourism conversion" despite nearby attractions (p24, p35).

**5. The mid-market is missing.** Mid-market accommodation "is effectively absent outside Stellenbosch" in the Winelands, where a "luxury-skewed product mix excludes mid-market and family segments" (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p47, p53). Accommodation is thin beyond Langebaan and Paternoster on the West Coast and thin at international grade along Route 62 (p62, p84). The report gives no bed count for the gap.

**6. Bookability fails first in the regions.** About 40% or more of the Metro's smaller operators lack online booking (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p32). Route 62 has the lowest online bookability of the six routes, and the West Coast route rates Gap on digital distribution and payments (p62, p84, p87).

blocks.caption: Only the Cape Peninsula route is rated ready for international visitors, and bookability or accommodation is the weak point on the rest.
blocks.source: Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p29, p30, p39, p40, p50, p51, p61, p62, p72, p73, p83, p84.

blocks.text: **7. The flagships are full in season.** Table Mountain Aerial Cableway queues run two to three hours at peak, Chapman's Peak suffers disruptions and the December to January peak "overwhelms transport and accommodation capacity" (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p28, p32). Cape Point and township attractions, by contrast, are underused (p24).

**8. Committed capital closes the air gaps, not the regional ones.** The Metro's pipeline exceeds R30bn, led by ACSA's R11.3bn airport overhaul and the R20bn V&A Granger Bay expansion, and George's R310m terminal doubles capacity by 2028 or 2029 (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p32, p43). Last-mile transit, small-operator bookability and township product remain unfunded in the Metro, as do inter-node transport and winter product on the Garden Route (p32, p43).

Port spending is not going to cruise. Cape Town's single berth runs at about 40% of a season capacity of 150 or more calls, with 83 calls and R1.79bn of impact in 2024/25 (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p110). Saldanha's R4bn upgrade is for iron ore, and the report's advice is to grow cruise "through product and marketing, not capital works" (p112).

blocks.title: What this means for the tree
paras: **Validates FA09, Accelerate tourism-enabling internal mobility.** Accessibility decays from 4.7 to 1.0 and public transport is absent beyond the Metro and the Garden Route (findings 1 and 3).
**Validates FA10, Support diversified route and product development, and FA11, Align visitor experience in-destination.** Strong assets in cold zones and a missing mid-market (findings 4 and 5).
**Validates FA12, Balance impact on nature-based attractions.** Flagships full at peak while alternatives are underused (finding 7).
**Supports FA03, Make the whole province findable and bookable.** Bookability fails first in the regions (finding 6).
**Supports FA07, FA08 and FA15.** Airport capital is committed; cruise needs product, not berths; regional gaps have no committed capital (finding 8).
